tells: Each quotation is introduced by name and then built on ('It is his own self that he worships', 'If even Paradise is not to be the goal, powers certainly are not'), the same inference-from-text move as 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses'; the only slip is 'the lecturer's own word' where Author A writes 'Sheikh Bahmanpour'

'This good life, hayat tayyiba, is in Sheikh Bahmanpour's reading a clean life' gives the term with an appositive gloss and names the Sheikh, and each gift gets its own paragraph with its verse placed, as in the reference
'The reward.' is a verbless fragment used as a mini-heading; Author A writes full sentences and links paragraphs with prose ('The second claim goes further')
'is in the lecturer's reading' and 'is of course what mystics are after': Author A always names 'Sheikh Bahmanpour' or 'the Sheikh' and would not keep a spoken 'of course' in a quotation

'The second gift is a different kind of life.' followed straight by the verse, and 'The third gift is peace.' tacked on at a paragraph's end: Author A says where the verse comes from ('promised in Surah al-Nahl to whoever acts righteously') and starts a new point in a new paragraph

'pure of the filth of this world ... without living in its filth ... concerns that infect everyone else': the repeated, heated imagery is more colourful than Author A's plain 'without being soiled by it'

The opening 'If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works' picks up the previous point, and 'A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of; a name means little...' reasons from the verse with a semicolon, as Author A does

The serial comma is dropped ('its range and its penetration and neither arrives at God'; 'absent from another and He has no partner'), and each quotation gets a measured gloss, both matching the reference's habits
'Imam Khomeini gives study its place, with a warning' leads into a named quotation, as in 'Imam Khomeini insists that...'; the circle sentence explains the Tabatabaʾi quotation in plain words

The cross-references ('Chapter One reached the same conclusion by a different road', 'Chapter Seven returns to that companion') work like the reference's 'as Chapter One shows'; the opening 'A light received in one heart can reach another' picks up the previous paragraph, and the diction is plain

'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim. Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk. Mutahhari explains why...': a whole paragraph that recaps what was just said; Author A moves on to the next step instead of summarising the last one

'...gave at the end of his first lecture: ʿirfan "is actually seeking and nothing else"': claim, colon and quotation stacked into one sentence; Author A would end the sentence and let the quotation stand, or bring it in with 'in his words'
'maʿrifah, the knowledge of God; and the love of God': a semicolon used to split a two-item list; Author A writes plain lists with no serial punctuation ('maʿrifah, knowledge and an ʿarif')

'...Himself" and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying that he worshipped God not from fear...': an and-chain that runs a quotation into a paraphrase; Author A gives the Imam's words their own introduced sentence

The definition is followed by the Sheikh's image ('the two things by which the friends of God fly'), 'the knowing of God and the love of God' keeps Author A's unpunctuated list and 'knowing' wording, and the closing recap follows the plain, stepwise style of the reference's introduction

'Tawhid is simple to say and very hard to grasp' and the contrast between fearing punishment and fearing Him are in Author A's plain explanatory register; the sentence-opening 'But' and the use of 'Allah' are mild doubts

'ordinary people, he says ... It is difficult, he says ... yet he says ... A human being, he says': the speech tag is used again and again; Author A uses 'he says' sparingly and names the Sheikh at the start
'He means this as a statement of what we were made for.': a vague sentence that restates the previous one; Author A would give the content directly
'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan.' opens a paragraph that summarises the chapter so far; Author A goes straight to the next step
'That doorway is open to people like us: ordinary people, he says, can also enter...': a claim, a colon and a reported claim stacked in one sentence
'The point is worth drawing out.': a stand-alone line of throat-clearing; Author A just draws the point out

'A person who has eaten enough can still feel hungry. They may be wrong to think that their body needs food. They cannot be wrong that they feel hungry.': a staccato run that ends on a neat antithesis, like an aphorism; Author A would fold this into one explanatory sentence after the Sheikh's remark
